planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into gritty, sharply drained soil; this western Chinese species tolerates more sun and lime than most daphnes but still resents transplanting once established.

directions: Native to scrubby, rocky slopes in Gansu, Qinghai, and Sichuan, this low, rounded deciduous shrub bears clusters of bright yellow, sweetly fragrant flowers along the stems in mid to late spring, followed by small red berries that, like all daphnes, are toxic if eaten. Grow it in lean, gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to very light shade, since it is more sun-tolerant than many of its woodland relatives but still fails in heavy or waterlogged ground. Site it where it can be left undisturbed, mulch with gravel to keep the crown dry, and prune only to remove dead wood right after flowering.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, acidic, well-drained soil in light shade; protect from hard freezes, as this subtropical species is far less cold-hardy than the deciduous Enkianthus of Japan.

directions: Unlike most enkianthus grown in temperate gardens, this evergreen, subtropical species from southern China, Hong Kong, and Vietnam flowers in winter, producing clusters of waxy, bell-shaped blooms in shades of pink, white, and red right around Lunar New Year, when potted specimens are traditionally sold and gifted across Cantonese communities as symbols of good fortune. Grow it in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in light shade with shelter from freezing wind, since it tolerates only light, brief frost. In warm-winter gardens it makes a handsome evergreen background shrub even outside its festival season.
sources: Hong Kong Herbarium (Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department)

planting.note: Direct sow or set divisions after frost danger in lean, dry, well-drained soil; thin or site carefully, since this species self-sows readily and is regulated as a noxious weed in some western states.

directions: Branching, hairy stems carry palmate, five- to seven-lobed leaves and flattened clusters of pale sulfur-yellow, five-petaled flowers from early to midsummer, a soft color break from the more common golden-yellow cinquefoils. It thrives in poor, dry, neglected soil and full sun, making it useful in wildflower plantings and informal dry gardens, but gardeners in the western United States should check local weed regulations before planting, since it naturalizes aggressively outside cultivated beds in parts of its introduced range. Deadhead before seed set if containment is a concern.

planting.note: Cold-stratify seed before sowing indoors; germination is slow and improved by a period of moist chilling. Transplant into lean, sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil after frost.

directions: One of the few white-flowered members of its genus, rock cinquefoil holds open, five-petaled white blooms above wiry stems and basal rosettes of pinnate, grey-green leaflets, native to rocky and calcareous slopes across Europe and the Caucasus. Plant in lean, sharply drained, lime-tolerant soil in full sun, where it is valued in rock gardens and scree beds for the color contrast it offers against the genus's usual yellows. It resists rot best in soil that dries between waterings and dislikes rich, heavy ground.

planting.note: Direct sow or divide established clumps in spring; set into humus-rich, well-drained soil at the edge of woodland or open ground.

directions: A low, slowly spreading mat-former native to dry grasslands and open woods of central and eastern Europe, white cinquefoil bears palmate leaves that are silky-silvered on the underside and sends up star-shaped white flowers just above the foliage in late spring. It suits woodland-edge groundcover, path edging, or the front of a border where its quiet texture can show against bolder neighbors. Give it light shade to full sun and soil that does not stay soggy, and divide congested patches every few years to keep them vigorous.

planting.note: Start indoors on the soil surface, since seed needs light to germinate; transplant after frost into sharply drained, limy soil in a rock garden or wall crevice.

directions: Native to rocky limestone slopes in the Caucasus, this compact bellflower produces nodding, pale lavender-grey bells held above soft, silvery-grey, hairy foliage through much of the summer, a muted color that reads differently from the typical saturated blues of garden campanulas. It is at its best in a rock garden, wall crevice, or scree bed where drainage is sharp and winter wet is minimal, since soggy soil is its chief enemy. Full sun and lean, gritty soil keep the mounds tight and free-flowering.

planting.note: Cold-stratify seed before sowing, then disturb roots as little as possible when transplanting; the species is monocarpic and resents being moved.

directions: Easily the oddest-looking campanula in general cultivation, this Alpine and Jura native sends up a dense, cylindrical spike of pale sulfur-yellow flowers atop a rosette of hairy, lance-shaped leaves, a color and form that sets it apart from the typical blue bells of the genus. It is monocarpic, spending its first one to two years as a rosette before flowering once and dying after seed set, so plan for a succession of plants if a continuous display is wanted. Grow in lean, sharply drained, lime-rich soil in full sun, conditions that mimic its native calcareous alpine meadows.
